planting.note: Sow fresh seed in early autumn with cold-moist stratification near 40F through winter; the bulblet forms underground the first season, with the first true leaf often not emerging until the following spring. Source bulbs or seed only through conservation-minded exchanges, never wild-collected, since this species is federally endangered.

directions: Among the most dramatic Turk's-cap flowers of any native lily, this species carries deep red to crimson tepals with a yellow central star, black spotting, and lime-green nectar furrows forming a secondary star, pollinated by hummingbirds. Plant in constantly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the edge of a bog garden or sphagnum bed in full sun to light shade, avoiding heavy summer irrigation that encourages bulb rot. This species is federally endangered and CITES Appendix I, so seed or bulbs are only ethically available through conservation-minded bulb exchanges, not general retail — growing it ex-situ carries genuine conservation value.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile

planting.note: Sow seed with double dormancy: 6-8 weeks warm stratification near 70F until bulblets form, then 4-6 weeks cold stratification near 35F, then grow on at 55-60F; plant bulbs in fall in dappled light under conifer or mixed-evergreen canopy.

directions: One of the showiest and most fragrant western native lilies, this species carries large, strongly recurved, pale-pink-to-lavender flowers with a yellow central stripe and scattered dark spotting on tall stems, standing out in a shaded woodland fragrance border. Site in dappled light under conifer or mixed-evergreen canopy in humus-rich but well-drained soil, matching its Klamath Mountains forest-understory habitat. It is uncommon rather than endangered, so nursery-propagated seed is reasonably findable through specialty native-bulb sources — never collect wild stock given its narrow range.

planting.note: Sow seed with the same double-dormancy pattern as other mountain lilies, then plant bulbs in a bog bed, stream edge, or irrigated meadow that stays wet through the growing season and gets real winter cold.

directions: A tall, stately subalpine wetland lily bearing up to 25 nodding, bell-shaped, yellow-to-orange flowers heavily flecked with red, pollinated by swallowtail butterflies, making it a dramatic streamside or bog-garden centerpiece considerably larger-flowered than the related Lilium parvum. It is best suited to a cool-summer garden with a bog bed, stream edge, or irrigated meadow planting that stays wet through the growing season and gets real winter cold, and will struggle in mild, dry-summer lowland gardens. It is taxonomically distinct and endemic to the Sierra Nevada and southern Cascades.
sources: Flora of North America / Jepson eFlora

planting.note: Sow seed with double dormancy, then plant bulbs in sandy, acidic, consistently moist-to-boggy soil within a cool coastal fog influence; avoid letting it dry out, especially in inland gardens.

directions: A genuine fogbelt collector's plant for coastal Northern California and Pacific Northwest gardens, this species carries striking nodding, bell-shaped, red-to-orange flowers strongly recurved at the tips, up to 13 per stem. It needs sandy, acidic, consistently moist-to-boggy soil within a cool coastal fog influence and is genuinely difficult outside that narrow niche, which is why it's uncommon in general cultivation. It is not federally or state listed for trade restriction, and specialty species-lily nurseries have carried true seed-grown stock alongside occasional availability through bulb exchanges.

planting.note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs in fall along a streambank or moist drainage edge in partial shade to full sun, in humus-rich soil that never fully dries out through the growing season.

directions: A Klamath-Siskiyou endemic subspecies of leopard lily with solid, uniformly yellow-orange-to-orange flowers rather than the two-toned coloring typical of the species, broad perianth segments, and yellow anthers spotted magenta and brown. It makes a natural companion planting to the already-present Vollmer's Lily subspecies for a complete regional bog-lily collection, tolerant of both sun and shade along drainages. Distinguish it in the garden from Vollmer's Lily by its solid-colored, not two-toned, orange flowers and broader tepals.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile
